claims.note: Pass 4 finding. The source's history note records the 1874 reduction (10 days → 6 days at the end of the session) and separately records the 119th Congress's removal of the last-six-days inclusion — but never affirmatively states the window was continuously part of the rule between those two data points. 'Had been part of the rule since 1874' is an inferential continuity claim over ~150 years that the source does not directly make. Rewritten to a source-anchored discrete historical fact: 'The rule's history note records that in 1874 the House cut the end-of-session limit from ten days to six.'

resolution: Pass 4 (this pass): headless hostile fresh read (runner-spawned Opus, no cross-model verifier). Decomposed the current draft prose into atomic claims and judged each in isolation against the sole registered source (hman-119-rule-xv). One new material-adjacent finding surfaced: the 'a window that had been part of the rule since the House cut it from ten days to six in 1874' phrase in the days section asserted continuous presence of the 6-day end-of-session window from 1874 to the 119th Congress — a ~150-year continuity inference the source never affirmatively states (source only records the 1874 reduction and the 119th removal; intermediate history is silent on the 6-day window specifically). Classified UNSUPPORTED / overgeneralization / minor. Rewrote the draft sentence to a source-anchored discrete historical fact: 'The rule's history note records that in 1874 the House cut the end-of-session limit from ten days to six.' Every other current-draft claim was re-verified verbatim against the source; no other new findings. Pass 3 (prior pass) applied the article-lane convergence contract: article ledgers do NOT carry framing/interpretive claims as visible style debt (unlike bill ledgers). Every previously-open UNSUPPORTED framing row was resolved by REWRITING the draft to a source-anchored form or CUTTING the sentence — never by hedging. Prior open flags fixed in pass 3: intro trade-off framing (three claims: 'trades away ... in exchange for speed', 'in return', 'rather than a simple majority'), 'That distinction changes the arithmetic on any day when attendance is short', 'the part where an out-of-date description is easiest to find'. Class-exhaustion sweep in pass 3 found and fixed additional siblings: 'If two-thirds agree, both things happen at once — the obstacles are set aside and the measure is passed' (metaphor), 'The reach of that is broader than it sounds' (editorial framing), 'which is why it can carry a measure past requirements that would otherwise stop it' (causal reasoning), 'It is not a universal tool' (editorial framing), 'The number that matters is two-thirds of the members voting' (editorial emphasis), 'The threshold is old' (editorial characterization), 'This is the part of the rule that has moved most' (comparative claim never made in source), 'Those three days are not an absolute cap' (editorial topic sentence), 'What cannot happen is as important as what can' (editorial framing), 'Almost nothing' (editorial characterization), 'Failing to reach two-thirds does not kill the measure' (topic-sentence inference), 'One asymmetry is worth knowing' (editorial framing), 'Suspension is one of several routes to the House floor' (editorial framing). Redundant topic-sentence paraphrases also removed in pass 3: 'Committee sign-off is not a prerequisite either', 'Whether a motion is entertained at all is the Speaker's call', 'The measure itself is not read out', 'The proponent keeps control until the vote begins', 'One motion to adjourn, and then the House votes'. H2 heading 'Why two-thirds instead of a majority?' rewritten to 'What vote does the motion require?' in pass 3 (removes 'instead of a majority' comparison). Every current-draft claim is bound to a verbatim source span in the sole registered source (hman-119-rule-xv). Zero open non-SUPPORTED rows. All prior fixes preserved as the regression baseline.
